name: Polypropylene-coated sheet (PP powder-coated spring steel)
aliases: Double-sided powder-coated PP spring steel sheet
summary: A purpose-built surface for the one filament nothing else will hold: polypropylene. A PP-based powder coating on flexible spring steel exploits like-sticks-to-like chemistry to grip PP without glue, tape or release agents, and incidentally handles PLA, PETG and TPU well. The same chemistry is its main hazard — a PP part pressed too hard into a PP coating can weld permanently, so first-layer calibration matters more here than on any other surface.
surface_makeup: Polypropylene-based powder coating applied to both faces of a flexible spring-steel carrier sheet, with an anti-corrosion layer beneath. The finish is a matte texture comparable to a satin PEI sheet. This is a formulated powder coating, not raw PP film or PP packing tape — the DIY alternatives it replaces. BuildTak's equivalent, Plus+ PP, is an adhesive-backed sheet pre-coated with a proprietary 'Bond PP' formula rather than a steel plate.

filament_compatibility.notes: The reason the sheet exists. No separation layer, no glue stick, no PP packing tape — the surface is formulated to bond PP directly. Prusa validates Prusament PP Carbon Fiber Black on it specifically. Get the first-layer Z right: this is the one material that can weld permanently to this coating.
Filled PP grades are the validated case; glass or carbon fill lowers shrinkage and makes large PP footprints far more practical than neat PP.

preparation: First use and routine prep are the same procedure: wipe the sheet with roughly 90% isopropyl alcohol while it is cold, before every print. If IPA alone is not cutting the grease — usually visible as a shiny patch where fingers have been — follow with dish soap and warm water, rinse, and dry completely; never leave the sheet damp or remount it wet, since the anti-corrosion layer protects the steel but does not make it waterproof. The step that actually determines success here is first-layer calibration, not cleaning. This surface is not meant to be forced into holding a part by over-squishing the first layer, and with PP that habit is actively dangerous, because PP-on-PP contact under pressure can fuse permanently. Dial the Z-offset with a dedicated first-layer test after mounting, and re-run it when swapping from a PEI sheet, since the coating thickness and effective datum differ.
cleaning: Cold IPA at around 90% for routine cleaning; dish soap and warm water for a degrease, dried fully before use. Never use acetone — it damages the coating, as with Prusa's other powder-coated sheets. Never put this sheet in a freezer: Prusa warns against it explicitly, which is a genuine departure from the freezer-release trick that is standard advice on PEI and steel plates, so unlearn that habit when you switch sheets. Avoid metal spatulas and any sharp-edged tool; the coating is a thin wearable layer rather than a hard ceramic-like film, and gouges become permanent dead spots. Do not use abrasives or scouring pads, which polish out the matte texture that provides part of the mechanical grip.
model_removal: Cold release by flexing the sheet, exactly as with any spring-steel system: let the bed cool, lift the sheet off the magnetic base by its tabs, and bow it progressively from one edge so the part peels off rather than popping all at once. Most parts should come free with a gentle flex — the coating's whole design intent is low peel adhesion, so if a part is genuinely fighting you, that is a signal about first-layer squish rather than a cue to apply more force. Keep sharp metal tools away from the surface; if a plastic scraper is needed, slide it in at a shallow angle at a corner. PP parts in particular deserve patience, because the failure mode when they do not release is not a scratch but a fused footprint that takes coating with it.
stuck_print_recovery: Start with the sheet off the magnet and flex it harder and from multiple directions — that resolves most cases. Then IPA wicked under the part perimeter, given a minute or two to creep in. Then unwaxed dental floss or thin wire sawed under the footprint, which applies shear rather than a point load and is the safest mechanical escalation. What you must not do is the freezer, which Prusa specifically prohibits for this sheet even though it is the standard trick elsewhere. Heat-then-slow-cool cycling to break stubborn PP-on-PP fusion is not documented and should be regarded as untested (unverified). The honest guidance from both Prusa's documentation and the broader community is that PP-coated surfaces are a prevention problem, not a recovery problem: a correctly set Z-offset and a bed that is not running hotter than needed will keep you out of this situation, and once PP has genuinely welded to a PP coating there may be no non-destructive way back.

damage_avoidance.reason: Prusa's PP sheet page states it directly: never clean the PP sheet with acetone, this will damage the surface. The same prohibition Prusa applies to its powder-coated PEI sheets applies here, and there is no occasional-use allowance of the kind granted to the smooth laminated sheet.

Prusa prohibits putting this sheet in the freezer. This is a genuine departure from the freezer-release trick that is standard advice on PEI and steel plates, so it is a habit to unlearn deliberately when switching sheets rather than a soft preference. Harder flexing and IPA wicking are the sanctioned escalations instead.

Prusa states the sheet is not scratch-resistant and to avoid metal spatulas with sharp edges. The PP coating is a thin wearable layer rather than a hard ceramic-like film, so a gouge is not a scratch in a durable surface but a hole through the working material, and it becomes a permanent dead spot.

The matte texture supplies part of the mechanical grip on a coating whose whole design intent is low peel adhesion, so polishing it out removes what little grip there is. Unlike powder-coated PEI, where fine abrasion is a documented reset on at least some brands, there is no published revival procedure for a PP coating.

damage_avoidance.item: Leaving the sheet wet, or soaking it
damage_avoidance.reason: Prusa's instruction is do not leave the sheet wet, because moisture compromises the anti-corrosion layer beneath the coating. That layer protects the steel; it is not waterproofing. Dry immediately after a soap wash and never remount a damp sheet on the magnet.

damage_avoidance.item: Over-squishing the first layer when printing PP
damage_avoidance.reason: The defining hazard of this surface and the reason it exists. Like sticks to like: PP-on-PP contact under first-layer pressure can fuse permanently, and the failure is not a scratch but a welded footprint that takes coating with it when it finally comes off. No heat-then-cool recovery for genuine PP-on-PP fusion is documented, so this is a prevention problem rather than a recovery problem.

damage_avoidance.item: All liquids, including IPA and plain water, on BuildTak Plus+ PP
damage_avoidance.reason: Product-dependent and directly contradictory within this entry. Prusa instructs an IPA wipe before every print on its powder-coated PP sheet; BuildTak's adhesive-backed Plus+ PP prohibits all solvents and all liquids including water, specifying a dry microfibre cloth only, because solvents damage the Bond PP coating and liquid at the perimeter creeps under the adhesive. Check which product you own before cleaning it.

Prusa publishes no numeric maximum for this sheet, so the ceiling in this entry is inferred from PP's normal 90-100 degC bed range plus headroom and is the least certain figure recorded for this plate. Running above the rated bed temperature is also named among the accelerators of coating wear generally.

damage_avoidance.item: Ammoniated window cleaner used to reduce tack
damage_avoidance.reason: Circulates as a community fix for the over-grippy PP variants some users report, and it is anecdotal, not vendor-sanctioned. It also runs against Prusa's framing of the surface as low-tack by design, which means a plate that needs de-tacking probably has a first-layer calibration problem instead. Ammoniated cleaners on a polyolefin coating are undocumented, and any residue left behind lowers adhesion unpredictably.

Prusa notes that some paper towels leave fibre traces on this sheet. Trapped fibres under a first layer read as adhesion failure and get misdiagnosed as coating wear; use a lint-free cloth for the pre-print IPA wipe.

lifespan_notes: An explicit consumable. Prusa states that surface coatings diminish over time and that its warranty covers manufacturing defects present on arrival, not wear or cosmetic damage from use. Expect the matte texture to polish smooth in the high-traffic centre first, showing up as prints that hold at the edges and lift in the middle. Wear is accelerated by metal tools, acetone or other solvents, and any over-adhesion event that pulls coating away in a patch. Being double-sided effectively doubles usable life — flip the sheet when the first face degrades. There is no recoating option; replace the sheet when adhesion no longer recovers after a proper degrease.

price.notes: Prusa's official double-sided PP Powder-Coated Print Sheet lists at USD 46.99. BuildTak Plus+ PP, the adhesive-backed alternative, spans USD 9.90 (A1 mini size) to USD 26.75 (Raise3D Pro3 size); the exact price of the ~254x254 mm Bambu P1/X1/A1 class was not captured, so the top of this range reflects the Prusa steel sheet rather than a like-for-like comparison.

additional_notes: Prusa's version is a double-sided powder-coated spring steel sheet mounting on the same magnetic bases as its PEI sheets (MK4, MK3.9, XL, CORE One). BuildTak Plus+ PP covers the same need in adhesive-film form and is cut for Bambu Lab (A1 mini, P1/P2/X1/A1/X2D), Prusa (MK3, CORE One), Creality (CR-10) and other beds — which is how Creality and Bambu owners get a PP surface at all, since neither vendor sells an official one. Bambu users otherwise improvise with PP packing tape over a textured PEI plate. The defining characteristic of this whole surface category is that like-sticks-to-like cuts both ways: the same chemistry that finally makes PP printable is what makes under-calibrated PP prints fuse irreversibly, and that trade-off is called out repeatedly in Prusa's own documentation. A secondary quirk worth knowing is that some users report the opposite problem — over-grippy PP variants — and wipe the sheet with window cleaner to reduce tack, which is anecdotal and not vendor-sanctioned.

provenance.conflicts: Prusa publishes no numeric maximum surface temperature for the PP sheet; the 110 degC ceiling recorded here is inferred from PP's normal 90-100 degC bed range plus headroom, not from a datasheet, and is the least certain number in this entry. The compatible-material list (PP, PLA, PETG, TPU) is stated positively; every 'avoid' rating here is inferred from the product page's warning that other materials tend to detach mid-print rather than from an explicit prohibition. PVB, TPE, COPE and PLA-CF are not addressed by any source and are extrapolated. This entry covers two physically different products under one id — Prusa's double-sided powder-coated spring steel sheet and BuildTak's adhesive-backed Plus+ PP film — which differ in mounting, price and cleaning rules (Plus+ PP prohibits all liquids including IPA and water, directly contradicting Prusa's IPA-before-every-print instruction); splitting them may be warranted. Whether BuildTak's Plus+ PP carries the same PP-on-PP fusion warning could not be verified, as some vendor pages returned fetch errors. Anecdotal community reports of over-adhesion needing a window-cleaner wipe conflict with Prusa's framing of the surface as release-oriented and low-tack. No evidence was found that Bambu Lab sells an OEM PP plate. The Duet3D thread cited returned 403 during research and its content is unverified; the Bambu forum thread was identified by title and context only.
